clue.text: Backward students tend 'to make mistakes

indicators.note: Backward tells us to read the word for students from its end to its start

parts.note: students are pupils

explanation.surface: A remark that slow learners are prone to errors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backward' looks like a description of the students, but it is the reversal signal: PUPILS read backwards gives SLIPUP. 'tend to' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: To slip up is to blunder or err, which is what making mistakes means.

clue.text: Noted movement 'in popular government

indicators.note: in says the answer sits within the letters of the next two words

explanation.surface: A notable shift in a government that people like.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noted' means written in musical notes: the answer runs across popuLAR GOvernment.
explanation.definitionFit: Largo is a slow musical tempo, and a piece marked so is a movement of a symphony or sonata.

clue.text: Nick Brook is cheap and gaudy

parts.note: to nick is to pinch, steal
a beck is a northern English word for a brook

explanation.surface: A man called Nick Brook is flashy and tawdry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick Brook' reads like a name; it is two verbs and nouns, PINCH and BECK. 'is' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinchbeck was a copper-zinc alloy imitating gold, so the word came to mean sham, flashy and tawdry.

clue.text: Tools for cabmen looking for fares?

definitions.text: Tools for cabmen looking for fares?

parts.words: Tools for cabmen looking for fares?
parts.note: cabmen ply for hire, so those who ply are named by the same word as a gripping tool

explanation.surface: Equipment taxi drivers need when touting for passengers.
explanation.walkthrough: Cabbies 'ply for hire'; one who plies would be a 'plier', the same word as the gripping tool.
explanation.definitionFit: Pliers are pincer-like hand tools, and the word also reads as 'those who ply', as touting cabmen do.

clue.text: Jocund signora

parts.note: Leonardo's portrait is known in Italy as La Gioconda, and jocund means cheerful, so the cheerful Italian lady is the famous sitter

explanation.surface: A cheerful Italian lady.
explanation.walkthrough: The painting's Italian title, La Gioconda, puns on 'jocund' (merry), the quality of her famous smile.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonardo's portrait is called La Gioconda in Italian, literally the jocund or merry woman.

clue.text: Quantitatively, very similar

parts.note: the phrase built on much, a word of quantity, means hardly different

explanation.surface: Two things almost the same in amount.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom repeats 'much', a word for quantity, hence 'Quantitatively'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means practically the same, with little to choose between them.

clue.text: Proverbially they go down well with cheese

definitions.text: Proverbially they go down well with cheese

parts.words: Proverbially they go down well with cheese
parts.note: things that fall easily are said to go down like skittles, and a cheese is the flat disc bowled at them

explanation.surface: Some foods are said to be eaten happily with cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: In old English skittles the missile was a flat wooden disc called a cheese; things that collapse in numbers 'go down like ninepins'.
explanation.definitionFit: The skittles game uses nine pins, knocked down with a disc called a cheese.

clue.text: Rocky 'rock

parts.note: a boulder balanced so that it rocks is a rocky rock, known in Cornwall by a special name

explanation.surface: An unsteady stone.
explanation.walkthrough: A logan, or logan stone, is a large balanced boulder that rocks at a push, found in Cornwall.
explanation.definitionFit: A logan stone is a balanced boulder that rocks when pushed.

clue.text: Do-gooder on the Jericho road

parts.note: in Christ's parable a traveller on the way to Jericho helps the robbed man others passed by

explanation.surface: A kind traveller met on the way to an ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: The parable in Luke's gospel tells of a man robbed on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho and helped by a passing stranger.
explanation.definitionFit: The Good Samaritan of the parable helped the man robbed on the road to Jericho, so the name means a helper.

clue.text: Grey Friar

parts.note: the grey habit gave one mendicant order of friars, founded by the saint of Assisi, its English nickname

explanation.surface: A friar dressed in grey.
explanation.walkthrough: In England the orders of friars were named by habit colour: Black (Dominican), White (Carmelite) and Grey, the followers of St Francis.
explanation.definitionFit: Followers of St Francis of Assisi were called Grey Friars in England after the colour of their habit.

clue.text: Sarah's'a good companion for a rainy day

definitions.text: Sarah's'a good companion for a rainy day

parts.words: Sarah's'a good companion for a rainy day
parts.note: Sarah's is Sarah's umbrella: Mrs Sarah ... in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit carried a baggy one, and her surname became a word for it

explanation.surface: Sarah praised as a pleasant friend when it rains.
explanation.walkthrough: Sarah Gamp is the drunken nurse in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit; her umbrella was so memorable that 'gamp' became British slang for an umbrella.
explanation.definitionFit: A gamp is an old British word for a large umbrella, named after Dickens's Sarah Gamp.

clue.text: Libertine is unwilling: to have a port

parts.note: loth (or loath) means unwilling
Rio de Janeiro is a Brazilian port, often called just Rio

explanation.surface: A rake who is reluctant to keep a port wine in the cellar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'port' suggests the drink, but here it is a harbour city, RIO. 'to have' only links the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Lothario, the seducer in Rowe's play The Fair Penitent, became a byword for a womanising rake.

clue.text: Room for young Peter to have a go

parts.note: Peter Pan is the boy who never grows up, forever young
to have a go is to try

explanation.surface: Space for a small boy named Peter to attempt something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peter' is J. M. Barrie's boy who never grew up, Peter Pan.
explanation.definitionFit: A pantry is a small storeroom for food, so it is a kind of room.

clue.text: The island sounds heavenly!

indicators.note: sounds says the island's name is said like the following word

parts.note: heavenly is to do with the sky, the heavens above

explanation.surface: An exclamation that an island has a divine-sounding name.
explanation.walkthrough: Skye is an island of the Inner Hebrides off western Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Skye is one of the Inner Hebrides, a Scottish island.

clue.text: It makes the cutting a mountain feature

explanation.surface: Something that both slices and shapes a peak.
explanation.definitionFit: The sharp edge of a blade does the cutting, and a narrow sharp ridge on a mountain is called by the same name.

clue.text: Renounce that crazy agent in Lincoln

indicators.note: in places the crazed agent within the name for Lincoln

parts.note: Abe is the short name of Abraham Lincoln

indicators.note: crazy says the letters of agent are scrambled

explanation.surface: Disown that deranged spy working inside Lincoln.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crazy' shuffles AGENT into NEGAT, which goes 'in' ABE (Abraham Lincoln) to give AB-NEGAT-E. 'that' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: To abnegate is to give up or deny oneself something, a formal synonym of renounce.

clue.text: Tend to come down to earth

explanation.surface: A habit of returning to reality.
explanation.definitionFit: To gravitate towards something is to be drawn or incline to it, and to be pulled down by gravity is to fall.

clue.text: Bouncer's speciality

parts.note: a nightclub doorman's main skill is throwing people out

explanation.surface: What a bouncing ball does best.
explanation.walkthrough: A bouncer is a doorman who removes troublemakers.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightclub doorman's job is throwing people out, which is expulsion.

clue.text: Twist a little woman 'of the upper class and find an animal

parts.note: a twist in a rope or hair is a kink
Jo March is one of the sisters in Alcott's Little Women
U is the old label for upper-class usage, as in U and non-U

explanation.surface: Bending a small upper-class lady out of shape and discovering a beast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little woman' is Jo from Louisa May Alcott's Little Women; U for upper class comes from the 1950s 'U and non-U' debate on British speech.
explanation.definitionFit: The kinkajou is a tree-dwelling mammal of Central and South America related to the raccoon.

clue.text: Sally's something of a nut

parts.note: ... Sally is a fairground figure, a target for thrown sticks, and the clue also hints that the relative's word is a nut rearranged

explanation.surface: A remark that a woman called Sally is slightly mad.
explanation.walkthrough: Aunt Sally is a British fairground and pub game in which sticks are thrown at a wooden head; 'nut' plays on head and on the letters of A NUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Sally is preceded by this relative's title in the name of the fairground target Aunt Sally.

clue.text: Matter for thought

parts.note: the grey matter of the head is what thinking is done with

explanation.surface: Something worth pondering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Matter for thought' reads as a topic to ponder, but here matter is the physical stuff that thinks.
explanation.definitionFit: The grey matter inside the skull is the organ used for thinking.

clue.text: Feverish, he knocks it back in small measure

indicators.note: in puts the turned word within the small measure

parts.note: cc, cubic centimetres, is a small measure of volume

indicators.note: back says the word it is turned round

explanation.surface: A man in a fever tosses off a little drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocks it back' suggests downing a drink, but 'back' reverses IT to TI, which goes 'in' CC (cubic centimetres) after HE: HE-C-TI-C.
explanation.definitionFit: Hectic originally described the flushed, feverish state of tuberculosis before coming to mean frantic.

clue.text: Put on a line, but not entirely of sound quality

indicators.note: but not entirely says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Hanging washing out, though not all of it, of good make.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition 'sound quality' is a noun phrase; the answer is an adjective, so the definition includes 'of'. The answer runs across puT ON A Line.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonal means relating to tone, the quality of a sound.

clue.text: The lads, we hear, have found 8 vixen

indicators.note: we hear says the answer is said like the lads' names

parts.note: the lads are two boys, Harry and Dan

explanation.surface: Some boys report that they have come across a female fox.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vixen' suggests a fox, but it is the shrewish woman. Said quickly, two lads' names, Harry and Dan, make the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a vixen and a harridan are bad-tempered, scolding women.

clue.text: Give out the voting for decapitation

indicators.note: decapitation means the head, the first letter, of the word for voting is cut off

parts.note: a ballot is a vote

explanation.surface: Announce the election result in favour of beheading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for decapitation' removes the first letter B from BALLOT.
explanation.definitionFit: To allot is to distribute or share out portions.

clue.text: A study of port

parts.note: a den is a private room for work, a study

explanation.surface: A piece of research into a harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A study of' reads like the title of a report; 'of' only links the pieces to the port.
explanation.definitionFit: Aden is a seaport in Yemen at the mouth of the Red Sea.

clue.text: "Awaits alike th' —— hour" (Gray)

parts.note: a line from Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard with its missing word, the one meaning the hour no one escapes

explanation.surface: A quotation from Thomas Gray with a word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: The full line of Gray's Elegy is 'The paths of glory lead but to the grave', preceded by 'Awaits alike th' inevitable hour'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gray's line describes death, the unavoidable hour that awaits everyone.

clue.text: Sound formalities indeed that we must look 'up to

indicators.note: Sound tells us the answer is said like the phrase that follows

parts.note: sealings are formalities in a deed, the seals fixed to a legal document

explanation.surface: Legal formalities that deserve our respect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'indeed' splits as 'in deed': the sealing of a legal deed is a formality, and SEALINGS is said like the answer. 'look up to' suggests admiration but is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: Overhead room surfaces are what we literally raise our eyes to.

clue.text: Gladiator has a case for putting up

definitions.text: Gladiator has a case for putting up

parts.words: Gladiator has a case for putting up
parts.note: a swordsman puts up his sword by returning it to its scabbard, the case he carries

explanation.surface: An arena fighter makes an argument for tolerating something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has a case for putting up' reads as arguing for something; in fact 'put up' is the old phrase for returning a sword to its scabbard.
explanation.definitionFit: A sword is put away into its scabbard, a close-fitting case.
